scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that a fast pace creates real problems, then argues it solves at least as many; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Modern life moves faster than ever, filled with instant messages, quick meals, and constant demands on our time.
Some people argue that this increasingly rapid pace of life causes more problems than it solves.
I agree that a fast pace brings real problems, but I do not believe it causes more harm than good, since the same speed also solves a great deal.
First, it is true that the rushing pace of modern life creates serious problems.
When people are always in a hurry, they suffer more stress, sleep less, and keep little time for family or rest.
For example, many workers today feel exhausted and anxious, still answering messages long after the working day should have ended.
This shows that a relentless pace can damage both our health and our closest relationships.
Hurrying also leads to careless mistakes, as people rush decisions they should have made slowly and thoughtfully.
A society that never pauses can gradually lose sight of what actually makes life meaningful.
In these ways, the rapid pace of life clearly does cause genuine harm.

sections.role: Body 2 — How speed also solves problems

sentences.text: Second, however, the same fast pace solves an enormous number of problems as well.
Today's speed allows food, medicine, and information to reach people far more quickly than in the past.
Consider how a fast ambulance, a quick internet search, or rapid communication can now save lives that would once have been lost.
Such speed gives ordinary people opportunities and freedoms that earlier, slower generations could only imagine.
A faster pace also lets us accomplish far more in a day, leaving room for both work and leisure when it is managed well.
Many of the very tools that hurry us along, such as quick transport and instant messaging, exist to make life easier.
The problem, then, lies less in speed itself than in how wisely we choose to use it.
In conclusion, the rapid pace of modern life undoubtedly brings stress and other real problems.
But it also solves countless problems and opens opportunities that slower times never offered.
Whether speed helps or harms us depends not on the pace alone, but on our ability to control it.
